Turbidity Sensor Calibration: NTU and FNU Units, ISO 7027 vs EPA 180.1, Formazin and StablCal Standards, Dilution and Troubleshooting

A turbidity reading is only as good as the standard used to calibrate it and the care taken with the sample cell. This page walks through units, methods, standards, dilution and field checks so your NTU values hold up in an audit.

NTU, FNU, FAU ISO 7027 vs EPA 180.1 Formazin and StablCal Dilution Calculator Troubleshooting Table

Turbidity sensor calibration sets the meter response against formazin or stabilised standards so readings in NTU or FNU are traceable. Learn the units, methods, dilution of 4000 NTU stock, calibration steps and common faults.

Hello everyone, today we are going to learn turbidity sensor calibration, from choosing the right standard to diluting formazin and fixing bad readings.

What Is Turbidity Sensor Calibration?

Turbidity sensor calibration is the process of setting a turbidimeter or online turbidity sensor so that its light scattering signal matches known formazin based standards, giving readings in NTU or FNU. It is done with a zero or low standard plus one or more higher standards, followed by verification with a check standard.

Quick Answer
  • Formazin is the primary turbidity standard, StablCal and polymer standards are common secondary options
  • EPA 180.1 uses white light at 90 degrees and reports NTU, ISO 7027 uses 860 nm light and reports FNU
  • Standard Methods formazin stock is 4000 NTU, diluted with very low turbidity water
  • After turbidity sensor calibration, a check standard should read within 10 % of its value
  • Bubbles, scratched cells and dirty optics cause most bad readings

If you are new to the measurement itself, start with our turbidity measurement guide, which covers nephelometry, sensor types and where turbidity is measured in a plant. This article is its calibration companion, so it focuses on standards, steps and errors.

YSI stresses that cuvettes for benchtop meters must be free of dust, fingerprints and scratches. That single point explains a large share of calibration problems in water treatment laboratories.

NTU vs FNU vs FAU: Turbidity Units

All common turbidity units are tied to formazin, but they describe different optical setups. YSI notes that NTU and FNU are often used interchangeably, yet they reflect different light sources and methods, so data from different methods should not be compared directly.

UnitFull NameLight SourceDetector AngleTypical Method
NTUNephelometric Turbidity UnitWhite light, tungsten lamp90 degreesEPA 180.1, Standard Methods 2130B
FNUFormazin Nephelometric UnitNear infrared LED, 860 nm90 degreesISO 7027 nephelometric
FAUFormazin Attenuation UnitNear infrared, 860 nm180 degrees, transmitted lightISO 7027 attenuation, high turbidity
FTUFormazin Turbidity UnitNot method specificVariesOlder general term

For drinking water compliance in many countries the reported unit is NTU, while submersible and online sensors often use the ISO 7027 infrared method and report FNU. YSI says its sensors have always used ISO 7027, so their values are the same whether labelled NTU or FNU.

Do You Know?

The EPA method requires a tungsten lamp at a colour temperature of 2200 to 3000 K and a detector centred at 90 degrees. Changing the lamp type changes the result, which is why white light and infrared meters can disagree on the same sample.

ISO 7027 vs EPA 180.1

EPA 180.1 (White Light)
  • Tungsten lamp, 400 to 600 nm response
  • Reports NTU, range 0 to 40 NTU before dilution
  • More sensitive to small particles
  • Coloured samples can read low
ISO 7027 (Infrared)
  • 860 nm LED source
  • Reports FNU, attenuation mode gives FAU
  • Colour effects are minimised
  • Stable LED, ideal for online sensors

EPA Method 180.1 states that its range is 0 to 40 NTU, and higher samples must be diluted before reading. It also warns that true colour, meaning dissolved substances that absorb light, lowers the reading, while finely divided air bubbles cause high readings.

The optics behave much like a spectrophotometer, except that the detector looks at scattered light instead of transmitted light. Pick one method for a site and keep it, so trend data stays comparable through every turbidity sensor calibration.

Primary vs Secondary Turbidity Standards

A primary standard is formazin prepared in the lab from hydrazine sulfate and hexamethylenetetramine, or a certified commercial formazin stock. A secondary standard is a stabilised liquid or gel, such as StablCal or AMCO AEPA polymer, whose value has been assigned against properly prepared formazin.

Lab Prepared Formazin

Made from hydrazine sulfate and hexamethylenetetramine, then diluted to working values.

Best for: Reference method, linearity checks
Primary
Hach StablCal

Stabilised formazin, ready to use, no dilution or Class A glassware needed.

Best for: Daily calibration in plants
Stabilised
AMCO AEPA Polymer

Styrene divinylbenzene beads that do not settle, value is instrument specific.

Best for: Field sensors, brand matched
Polymer
Gel or Sealed Vial Standards

Sealed secondary standards for quick daily checks of a meter.

Best for: Verification only
Check

Hach states that StablCal is made from the same 4000 NTU formazin stock and polymer as traditional formazin, is approved for USEPA reporting and meets ISO 7027. It is guaranteed for 24 months from manufacture, bottles should be used within 30 days of opening, and stated accuracy is plus or minus 5 %.

Myth: Any polymer standard works on any meter
Fact: YSI warns that only brand matched AMCO AEPA standards read their label value on its sensors
Myth: DI water is a perfect zero
Fact: YSI notes DI or distilled water can read up to 1 NTU, so use a certified zero standard for low range work
Myth: Lucite blocks are fine for calibration
Fact: EPA 180.1 forbids solid standards for calibration because surface scratches change the value
Myth: Polymer standards can be diluted like formazin
Fact: YSI says AMCO AEPA standards typically should not be diluted
Quick Tip

Never use a secondary gel or sealed vial for turbidity sensor calibration if the manufacturer lists it only as a verification standard. Use it to check the meter between calibrations and log the reading.

How to Dilute 4000 NTU Formazin

The North Carolina DEQ procedure for Standard Methods 2130 makes 4000 NTU stock by dissolving 1.000 g hydrazine sulfate in 100 mL water and 10.00 g hexamethylenetetramine in 100 mL water. Mix 5.0 mL of each, let it stand 24 hours at 25 plus or minus 3 °C and store it in amber glass, where it stays stable for up to a year.

Hydrazine sulfate is a carcinogen, so wear gloves and work in a fume hood, or simply buy certified stock. Use water filtered to 0.1 µm or finer, and the DEQ procedure requires dilution water to read 0.02 NTU or less.

Formazin Dilution Calculator
Volumes to Mix
Pipette 0.50 mL of stock and add 99.50 mL dilution water to make 100 mL (factor 200)
Solved example: 20 NTU from 4000 NTU stock
C1 × V1 = C2 × V2
V1 = 20 × 100 ÷ 4000
V1 = 0.50 mL stock
Water = 100 minus 0.50 = 99.50 mL
Dilution factor = 4000 ÷ 20 = 200

This is the same C1V1 = C2V2 rule used in any chemistry dilution calculator. For volumes under 1 mL, make an intermediate 400 NTU standard first, since a 10 times step with Class A pipettes is far more accurate than one tiny transfer.

Quick Tip

EPA 180.1 asks for fresh stock each month and fresh dilute standards each day. Formazin settles, so invert the bottle gently before every pipetting instead of shaking it into foam.

Advertisement

Turbidity Sensor Calibration Procedure

1
Warm up and clean
Switch on the meter for the time given in its manual and clean the optics or sample cells with lint free tissue.
2
Prepare standards
Use fresh formazin dilutions or in date StablCal standards that bracket the expected sample range.
3
Zero or low point
Read a certified zero or low standard, not plain DI water, for low range drinking water work.
4
Upper points
Read each higher standard in the order the manufacturer gives, wiping and indexing each cell.
5
Accept calibration
Check that the meter accepts the slope and record any warning before saving.
6
Verify
After turbidity sensor calibration, read a check standard that agrees within 10 % per EPA 180.1.
7
Record
Log standard lot numbers, expiry, as found and as left values in the calibration record.

Records matter in turbidity sensor calibration because auditors look for traceability back to formazin, as our guides on the calibration traceability chain and as found and as left values explain. Good records also show drift and support your measurement uncertainty budget.

For an online sensor, turbidity sensor calibration is usually done in a calibration cylinder or cup supplied by the maker. YSI warns that a smaller vessel lets the sensor see the cup bottom, which raises the calibration offset and gives negative readings in clean water.

How Often Should a Turbidity Meter Be Calibrated?

EPA 180.1 asks for a performance check after daily calibration, after every tenth sample and at the end of the run, with linearity verified every six months. Many plants follow the meter manual for full calibration, often quarterly for online sensors, and verify daily or weekly.

Set your own turbidity sensor calibration interval from drift history, as described in our article on calibration interval determination. A sensor that always passes verification can move to a longer interval, while one that keeps failing needs cleaning or repair first.

Turbidity Sensor Calibration Troubleshooting

SymptomLikely CauseFix
Readings high and jumpyAir bubbles in sample or cellDegas, let sample stand, tap cell gently
Calibration rejectedOld or settled formazinInvert gently, make fresh dilutions
Negative readings in clean waterDI water zero or small cal vesselUse certified zero and correct cup
Low readings on coloured waterColour absorbing light in white light meterUse ISO 7027 infrared method
Drift between checksFouled window or worn wiperClean optics, replace wiper

The NC DEQ procedure adds that a cold sample can fog the vial in a warm humid room, so warm it slightly and remix before reading. It also recommends degassing samples even when no bubbles are visible, using a partial vacuum, an ultrasonic bath or gentle heat.

  • Standards in date and bottles opened less than 30 days ago
  • Sample cells unscratched, clean and handled only at the top
  • Cells indexed to the same orientation every time
  • Dilution water verified at 0.02 NTU or less
  • Check standard within 10 % after calibration
  • Lot numbers and results written in the log

Plants that run several analysers, often fed by one sample conditioning system, calibrate turbidity together with other water quality sensors. Our guides on pH meter calibration buffers, conductivity cell constant calibration and dissolved oxygen sensor calibration follow the same discipline.

Online turbidity sensors usually send 4 to 20 mA to the control system, so after calibration confirm the scaling with our 4 to 20 mA conversion calculator. Then check that SCADA shows the same value, as covered in SCADA in water treatment.

Do You Know?

EPA 180.1 sets reporting resolution by range, for example to the nearest 0.05 NTU from 0 to 1 NTU and the nearest 0.1 NTU from 1 to 10 NTU. Reporting more digits than that suggests a precision the method does not support.

Filtered water turbidity is a key indicator of how well the water treatment process is removing particles. That is why careful turbidity sensor calibration on filter outlets protects public health.

Turbidity Sensor Calibration FAQ

How do you calibrate a turbidity sensor?

Clean the optics, warm up the meter and read a certified zero or low standard first. Then read each higher formazin or StablCal standard in the order the manual gives and accept the new slope.

Finish by reading a check standard that must agree within 10 percent. Record the lot numbers and results so every turbidity sensor calibration can be traced back later.

What is the standard used for turbidity calibration?

Formazin is the primary reference standard for turbidity worldwide. It is a polymer suspension made from hydrazine sulfate and hexamethylenetetramine with a stock value fixed at 4000 nephelometric units.

Stabilised formazin such as Hach StablCal and polymer standards such as AMCO AEPA are approved secondary options. They save preparation time but must suit your instrument and stay within their expiry date.

What is the difference between NTU and FNU?

NTU comes from a white light nephelometer with a tungsten lamp and a 90 degree detector, as in EPA 180.1. FNU comes from an 860 nm infrared source with a 90 degree detector, as in ISO 7027.

Both are referenced to formazin, so values are often close on clean water. They can differ on coloured samples or particles of unusual size, so do not mix the units in one data set.

Can I use distilled water as zero for a turbidity meter?

You can for higher ranges, but it is not a true zero. YSI notes that DI or distilled water can read up to 1 NTU, which matters on drinking water samples below that level.

For low range work use a certified zero standard or water filtered to 0.1 micron. Otherwise the calibration offset shifts and clean samples may show negative readings.

How long is formazin standard stable?

Lab prepared 4000 NTU stock stored in amber glass can stay stable for up to a year according to the NC DEQ procedure. EPA 180.1 is stricter and asks for new stock each month and fresh dilute standards each day.

Low value dilutions deteriorate quickly, which is why stabilised products exist. Hach guarantees StablCal for 24 months from manufacture and advises use within 30 days of opening.

Why does my turbidity meter give unstable readings?

Air bubbles are the most common cause, and EPA 180.1 notes that they make readings high. Scratched or dirty sample cells, condensation on cold vials and settling particles also cause unstable values.

Degas the sample, wipe the cell with lint free tissue and index it the same way each time. If readings still wander, clean the optics and repeat the verification.
